> 「若人满三千大千世界七宝以用布施……若复有人，于此经中受持，乃至四句偈等，为他人说，其福胜彼。」

The eighth section stages a comparison, and comparison is the oldest teaching device in the sutras.

On one side: a person fills the entire cosmos — a billion worlds — with the seven precious substances and gives it all away. On the other: a person receives four lines of this text, holds them, and explains them to someone else.

The second is said to be greater. Not equal. Greater.

## 三千大千世界 is a rhetorical maximum, not a map

The old cosmology multiplies: one world, a thousand of those, a thousand of those again, a thousand again. The number is deliberately beyond imagining.

The point is not cosmology. The point is to remove the ceiling from the first side of the comparison — to make the material gift as large as the language allows, so that the second side cannot win by arithmetic. It has to win by kind.

## 受持 is two verbs

受: to receive the meaning. 持: to hold it, not to forget it, to let it calibrate the mind.

This is not reading. A person can read this text every morning for ten years and never once 受持 it, because receiving means letting the sentence act on something. The section's comparison is between a gift of things and a transmission of seeing — and the second requires that someone actually take it in.

## 福德即非福德性

须菩提's reply to the first question is already the whole method: yes, enormous — because that merit is not a merit-nature, therefore it is called great.

The formula again: affirmation, cancellation, conventional naming. Merit functions enormously; it has no nature to hold; therefore we can speak of it as great without it becoming a possession.

Which prepares the comparison. If merit were a substance, more of it would be better, and the material gift could be beaten only by a bigger gift. Because merit is a functioning, the comparison can be between kinds of functioning rather than amounts.

## 皆从此经出 is about the content, not the paper

"All buddhas and their enlightenment come forth from this sutra." Read flatly, this makes a printed object the parent of every buddha — bibliolatry.

The book's correction: what comes forth is the principle the text carries — non-abiding prajñā, the path of not standing on anything. The paper is a vehicle. A vehicle is not a source.

The same correction is then applied to the word "Buddha-dharma" in the very next sentence: 所谓佛法者，即非佛法. What is called the buddha-dharma is not the buddha-dharma. Even the name of the teaching is subject to the rule.

## What the section is not saying

It is not saying stop giving things. The first side of the comparison is a genuine good — it is placed there as a real good, then exceeded.

And it is not offering a rate of exchange. The trap is explicit: read this and think *so expounding four lines earns more merit than donating a fortune* — that thought is itself the abiding, and it collapses the merit into something countable in the same motion.

The comparison is between giving that ends with the object handed over and giving that changes how the receiver sees. The second keeps working after the hand is empty.

## The test

Look at what you are counting.

Money given, hours volunteered, posts published, people helped, years practiced. All fine things. Now check whether any of them has become a number you are keeping.

If you find one, the eighth section's comparison has done its work: you have discovered that you were comparing quantities where the sutra compares kinds.
